title: Expensive cars stop less for pedestrians
sources: Piff, Stancato, Cote, Mendoza-Denton, Keltner (2012). Higher social class predicts increased unethical behavior. PNAS 109(11):4086-4091. doi:10.1073/pnas.1118373109. PMC3306667.

Study 2 (full text, PMC): 152 drivers, marked crosswalk of a busy one-way road, San Francisco Bay Area, June 2011; confederate pedestrian waiting to cross; vehicle status coded 1-5 by make, age, appearance; 34.9% failed to yield; higher vehicle status significantly predicted not yielding (b=0.39, P<0.05). Study 1: 274 drivers, four-way stop, 12.4% cut off other vehicles, also higher in high-status cars.

lines.text: The more expensive the car, the less likely it is to stop for you.
In California, psychologists placed a pedestrian at a marked crosswalk.
They watched one hundred fifty two drivers and rated every car, from old and cheap to new and luxurious.
About one in three drivers did not stop.
And the fancier the car, the more likely the driver was to drive straight through.
Even after accounting for the driver's age, sex, and the time of day.
The researchers' idea: wealth makes the rules feel optional.
They call it the entitlement of the upper class.
